Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva said: "I wish to joyfully proclaim the four great vows. What are these four?"
First, to shelter and nourish all sentient beings,
like a bridge or a boat ferrying people across without weariness.
Second, to encompass all phenomena, like the vast void.
Third, may my own body be like a medicinal tree,
such that whoever hears [my name] shall have all their ailments and sufferings completely removed.
Fourth, when I attain Buddhahood in the future, may I...
The sentient beings he delivers are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River;
this is the bodhisattva’s mind of vast salvation.
Thus it is with the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha.
I wish to joyfully expound upon the pure and wondrous practices cultivated by Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas for the purification of their Buddha-lands.
There are four matters. What are these four?
First, sacrificing oneself to benefit others and rescuing all living beings;
second, not giving rise to grief or distress regarding gain and loss, praise and blame;
third, maintaining integrity and purity without lust, with preceptual conduct as pure as a white lotus.
Fourth, when I shall become a Buddha in a future age,
all sentient beings in that land will achieve sublime conduct such that there will be no distinction between humans and devas.
This constitutes the pure and wondrous practice for the adornment of a bodhisattva’s buddha-field.
Furthermore, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva,
wishing to joyfully explain it, spoke of the four means of attraction (saṃgrahavastu) of a bodhisattva.
What are the four? First,
the bodhisattva practices the six pāramitās while simultaneously transforming others and rescuing all beings.
Second, they give rise to a mind of compassion and nurture all living beings.
Third, they benefit themselves and others, bringing profit to both self and other.
Fourth, when there are those suffering from illness, their hearts feel pity for them as if looking upon their own infants.
These are the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) by which a bodhisattva gathers sentient beings.
These are the sublime and virtuous merits by which a bodhisattva extensively benefits sentient beings and gathers a pure buddha-field.
Thus spoke the Bodhisattva Rescuer and Deliverer.
Furthermore, there is a desire to explain the four great vows,
which are not shared with the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
What are these four?
First, may my mind be like the great earth: just as all grasses,
trees, thickets, and sprouts grow by depending upon it,
while the earth harbors neither hatred nor affection.
Second, may my mind be like a bridge or a boat,
ferrying sentient beings across without ever becoming weary.
Third, may my mind be like the great ocean.
Fourth, may my body be like the great ocean, which receives the currents of all rivers without overflowing; and may my body be like empty space,
encompassing all things just as the *dharmatā* does.
These are the four great vows of a bodhisattva,
which are not shared with śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
Thus spoke the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla.
I wish to eloquently explain that there are eight matters concerning the sublime conduct of a bodhisattva. What are these eight?
First, a bodhisattva dwells in a world of five corruptions.
First, one rescues sentient beings without becoming weary or disheartened.
Second, upon seeing sentient beings undertaking meritorious deeds, one protects, assists,
and supports them without giving rise to a defiled mind.
Third, seeing others commit evil, one earnestly exhorts and admonishes them so that they may abandon it.
Fourth, toward those who encounter calamities and hardships, one provides relief and compassion, just as a mother loves her child.
Fifth, when there are those who come seeking help, he does not spare even his own body or life.
Sixth, when there are places of calamity and distress, he supports and guides them so that they may escape their hardships.
Seventh, seeing those with wrong views, he feels compassion for them and earnestly exhorts them so that they may attain right view.
Eighth, they nurture all sentient beings as if they were their own infants.
They take all their merits and bestow them entirely upon others,
dedicating them together toward unexcelled bodhi.
These are the eight matters by which a bodhisattva benefits immeasurable sentient beings.
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta wishes to joyfully explain that there are four matters by which a bodhisattva benefits sentient beings with a mind free from weariness.
What are the four? First,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva relinquishes his own happiness and bestows it upon sentient beings.
Seeing others suffer as if it were no different from oneself,
one’s compassionate heart flows with such pity that its pain pierces to the very marrow of the bones.
Second, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva establishes great bridges and boats at places where beings are submerged and drowning.
They ferry sentient beings across without weariness or fatigue.
Third, within the ocean of birth and death where sentient beings swirl in eddies,
the bodhisattva-mahāsattva takes them firmly by hand and leads them to the further shore.
Fourth, knowing that all sentient beings throughout the past and the present are like illusions and transformations;
though they have realized this principle, they never tire of delivering others.
These are the four matters by which a bodhisattva benefits and rescues all living beings.
The Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta, wishing further to speak with joy, said:
"Whoever is able to perform the work of a Buddha within the bequeathed Dharma of Śākyamuni Buddha, we eight shall constantly provide protection and guardianship for them."
The *Vibhāṣā* states that there are four matters; what are these four?
First, to recollect immeasurable suffering and to see the suffering of sentient beings as no different from one's own.
Second, the merit of the precepts we ourselves uphold.
They give everything away in charity to sentient beings,
dedicating it together for the sake of unsurpassed bodhi.
Third, they are able to endure hardships and bear the burden of all sentient beings until they reach the other shore.
Fourth, he arouses the minds of all sentient beings,
just as a compassionate father thinks of his children without distinction.
This is the pure and sublime practice by which a bodhisattva benefits both himself and others.
The Bodhisattva Dṛḍhavīrya further desired to joyfully explain that there are four matters regarding the sublime conduct of a bodhisattva. What are these four?
First, may I always be born in worlds where no Buddha resides,
just as the sun and moon travel across Jambudvīpa to dispel its darkness.
Second, may I be like one using a golden probe to clear away the cataracts of the eyes, so that they may behold the light.
Third, they act as great medicinal trees such that all sentient beings who catch their fragrance have their suffering and illness eliminated.
Fourth, they constantly expound the Dharma like the falling rain of the Dharma.
From their initial sprouting through growth to the ripening of fruit, they all give rise to the unsurpassed mind of bodhicitta.
These are the four great solemn vows of a bodhisattva.
I, Mañjuśrī, now wish to speak these sublime verses.
May this sutra circulate widely, so that sentient beings may have no doubts;
the profound and wondrous Dharma taught by the assembly of the seven Buddhas and bodhisattvas,
and the speech of the devas, nāga kings, and spirits, is truly most extraordinary.
This is the spell of the Pure and Sublime Conduct.
For those who transcribe, read, and recite it to protect the nation and the practitioner, they shall surely join the assembly of the thousand Buddhas.
Now, the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha wishes to speak two and a half verses.
One should praise those who transcribe [the scriptures], those who transcribe and recite them,

their words are elegant and beautiful, wondrously excellent and inexhaustible.
Just as the waters of the great ocean are deep and vast, beyond measure or end,
so too are the merits of this person, exceeding even those by many billions.
Now I, Mañjuśrī, wish to speak one verse and a half.
For all classes of sentient beings, there is none who can awaken them from that realm of lustful ghosts;
only I am able to rescue and deliver them, forever severing the root of birth and death,
so that they may universally abide in the bliss of quiescent extinction.
This single verse spoken by the Brahma King:

"I have constantly practiced the four immeasurables; Now coming here, I hear these wondrous words, Which rescue sentient beings from the suffering of birth and death, So that they shall forever no longer have grief, affliction, or distress."
The King of Tuṣita Heaven now wishes to speak one and a half verses:
"In the past, I encountered various Buddhas And attained rebirth in Tuṣita as a Heavenly King.
Now that I have been able to hear this single wondrous word, My mental obscurations are resolved and my eye of wisdom opened."
If there are sentient beings who hear this but once with their ears, they shall not fall into the three miserable realms but ascend to the Brahma Heaven.
The King of the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations wished to speak half a verse,
yet he heard that in this Jambudvīpa there were great bodhisattvas and others.
He expounded the subtle and profound meaning, and my heart was filled with great joy;
the seeds of birth and death were forever uprooted, and I attained entry into the Hall of Nirvāṇa.
These two and a half verses were spoken by the Heavenly King Sunirmita.
I have heard that throughout Jambudvīpa, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas each proclaim wondrous practices,
the four means of integration, and their great vows;
having heard these words, the eyes of my mind have opened wide.
May the hosts of devas obtain this pure faculty of the eye,
forever sever the stream of birth and death, and universally attain entry into Nirvāṇa.
Then King Yama, wishing to speak a verse like that of a wish-fulfilling jewel, said:
"We have long dwelt in the celestial palaces, weary of the suffering of birth and death within the three realms.
When shall we, like a snake shedding its old skin, forever attain the bliss of quiescent nirvāṇa?
The King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven then wished to speak half a verse.
Having long dwelt within birth and death, You grew weary of and renounced the mire of desire;
Arousing great compassion, you deliver beings from the suffering of birth and death,
And forever liberate them from the cycle of birth and death, Enabling them to enter the city of Nirvana.
The Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra wished to speak these four verses:
"Among the Four Great Heavenly Kings, I am the foremost;
Though I am a heavenly king, I have not escaped the suffering of ghosts and spirits."
I became a king of the ghost spirits, Having already passed five hundred years;
Constantly galloping to and fro, I deliver and save all living beings.
Alas! In past lives, I once served as a king among men.
If one governs and transforms others without recourse to principle, One will now take the form of a king of ghosts.
Furthermore, I pray that all kings Will govern state affairs with rectitude and refrain from acts of greed and corruption;
Otherwise, they shall again receive the bodies of spirits and ghosts.
The Heavenly King Virūpākṣa wished to speak one and a half verses:

Although I am now a king of ghosts and spirits, I still undergo the suffering of ghosts and spirits.
The Heavenly King Virūḍhaka wished to speak three verses:
"Now that I act as a king of ghosts and spirits, I have attained liberation from the sufferings of the three miserable realms."
Having traversed the four continents to save those suffering from illness,
he recalls his past lives when he was once a king among men;
through negligence and attachment to the five desires, he has now received the body of a ghost-king.

may he deliver all sentient beings so that they universally attain the bliss of nirvana.
King Vaiśravaṇa wished to speak one and a half verses.
In the past, I cultivated bodhi; for the sake of sentient beings, I became a king of ghosts.
Sentient beings have long dwelt in the darkness of ignorance; with a golden probe, I opened their eyes.
Once the eye of wisdom was opened, they were delivered from birth and death; having crossed over birth and death, they ascended to nirvana.
The Naga King Nanda wished to speak two and a half verses:

having heard of the various Bodhisattvas, each speaks of wondrous practices."
All the devas, nāgas, and spirits listen with their ears pricked;
the hosts of devas and the hosts of nāgas rejoice beyond measure.

I pray for the power of wisdom To destroy this darkness of ignorance."
Rescuing all from calamities and hardships, Transcending the stream of birth and death.
The Naga King Sagara wished to speak two verses:

Those who were stingy with their treasuries now receive the bodies of dragon kings;

governing and transforming them by means of the True Dharma, and never again undergo the state of a dragon.

"Residing here in the dragon palace, I am weary of the dragons' foul and rancid stench;

All the humans and devas within the three realms are likewise thus;
they take pleasure in the prison of the three realms as a pig does not loathe its latrine.
Alas, how deeply pitiable! They do not know to seek liberation.
The Naga King Utpala now wishes to speak five and a half verses:
"In a past life, I was born into a Brahmin family in Jambudvīpa;
I was intelligent and possessed great wisdom."
At that time, there was a neighboring king who sent a daughter to marry me.
This woman was not chaste; she had a secret affair with another man.
When I caught her in the act, I had her executed in the marketplace.
At that time, I despised and loathed him, sending him back to his own country;
contemplating the foulness and corruption of desire, I left the household life to practice the Right Path.
Yet, I again encountered evil associates and did not meet with virtuous companions.
I lured many courtesans there; at that time, filled with remorse and resentment, I took up a blade and cut my own throat.
Having endured the sufferings of the three miserable realms, I have since received this dragon body—its extreme agony is beyond description.

As the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha has taught, sentient beings have five kinds of lack of faith.
First, doubt regarding the Buddha; second, doubt regarding the Dharma;
third, doubt regarding the Saṃgha;
fourth, doubt that all phenomena are not real; fifth, giving rise to doubt and lack of faith toward the true Dharma.
Sentient beings possess five kinds of faculties of faith that enable them to attain the path of arhatship.
The first is faith that the Buddha is definitively and perfectly awakened.
Second, they have faith in the Jewel of the True Dharma with absolute certainty and without doubt.
Third, they have faith in the Sangha of bhikṣus as a field of merit that is excellent and substantial.
Fourth, regarding all correct practices—precepts, concentration, and wisdom—they do not give rise to doubt or uncertainty.
Fifth, one does not give rise to a mind of attachment when seeing worldly phenomena.
These five roots of faith can uproot the five doubts,
enable the attainment of the Jewel Banner Samādhi, and allow one to manifest in this body and attain the Way.
The first, the Radiance-Emitting Samādhi, can sever existence in the hells;
the Stainless Samādhi can sever existence as a hungry ghost;

the Samādhi of Radiance can sever existence in Pūrvavideha;
the Samādhi of the Mirage of Flames can sever existence in Jambudvīpa.
The white samādhi can sever existence in Godānīya;
the blue samādhi can sever existence in Uttarakuru;
the yellow samādhi can sever existence among the Four Heavenly Kings.
The black samādhi can sever existence in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven;
the red samādhi can sever existence in the Yāma Heaven;
the wondrously virtuous samādhi can sever existence in the Tuṣita Heaven.
The Samādhi of Extended Virtue can sever existence in the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations;
the Samādhi of Sound can sever existence in the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Emanations;
and the Samādhi of Sublime Goodness can sever existence in the First Dhyāna.
The Samādhi of Attaining Joy can sever existence in the second dhyāna;
the Samādhi of White Color can sever existence in the third dhyāna;
the Samādhi of Thunderous Sound can sever existence in the fourth dhyāna.
The samādhi of sublime goodness can sever existence in the Anāgāmin heaven;
the samādhi of emptiness can sever existence in the sphere of infinite space;
the samādhi of non-conceptualization can sever existence in the sphere of infinite consciousness.
The Resonance-Transformation Samādhi can sever existence in the sphere of nothingness;
the Jewel-Heap Samādhi can sever existence in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
These are the twenty-five great samādhis.

When Śākyamuni Buddha appeared in the world,
he delivered liberation to eighteen thousand and ninety-four people.
His first teaching was given in the Heaven of Control over Others' Emanations (Paranirmita-vaśavartin).
The second turning of the wheel of Dharma took place in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī;
the third turning of the wheel of Dharma took place in the city of Rājagṛha;
and the fourth turning of the wheel of Dharma took place in the kingdom of Kāśī.
He delivered seven thousand arhats to liberation.
His fifth discourse was given in Śrāvastī;
his sixth discourse was given in Rājagṛha.
He delivered the woman Gautamī.
His seventh teaching was given in the kingdom of Kapilavastu,
where he delivered King Śuddhodana.
The eighth teaching was given in Rājagṛha;
it consists of a mixed doctrine of the three vehicles.
The ninth teaching was given in the kingdom of Magadha, where he converted King Bimbisāra.
The tenth teaching was given in the kingdom of Kuśinagara.

He delivered liberation to hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis—immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable beings. Below this, the phrase "jiànzhě cài shēng zhì gǔ" (the builder, the vegetable, the growth, and the ancient) appears; however, it is noted that this is absent in the original *Bìdān* (Vibhāṣā).
"Building" refers to the sprouting of vegetables, when yin and yang also grow.
"Clearing away" refers to the essence of succession and transformation.
"Filling" means that the spirits and deities have received their offerings and there is no further surplus.
"Equilibrium" (*ping*) means that the Yang energy is coagulated and remains without increase or decrease.
"Stability" (*ding*) means that spirits and deities meet and evil energies do not circulate.
"Grasping" (*zhi*) means that Yin energy is excessive while Yang energy is deficient. "Breaking" (*po*) refers to the discussion of resolving the entanglement when Yin and Yang intersect.
"In Wei (Peril), the window of Heaven opens and the gate of Earth closes.
In Cheng (Completion), Yang energy is sufficient and Yin energy flows alongside it; thus it is named 'Completion.
In Shou (Gathering), Yang energy circulates and Yin becomes level, causing sprouts to emerge; therefore, it is called 'Gathering.'"
"Opening" (kāi) means that the yin nature opens so that yang qi emerges; thus it is called "opening.
"Closing" (bì) refers to the celestial window and the terrestrial gate, which are solemnly sealed so that the myriad deities cannot pass; thus it is called "closing."

Form them into a ball; for a man, first place it under the left armpit, and for a woman, first place it under the right armpit.

I am Hārītī, daughter of the spirits;
I shall now proclaim a divine mantra to protect sentient beings,
eliminating their false views and causing them to attain right view.
To squander family wealth to prepare delicacies for these worldly demons and goblins is not as good as sacrificing to a dog to serve as a guardian.
Now I shall explain the correct truth to you.
Simply by using flowers, incense, ghee, milk, and rice porridge to express one’s respectful devotion to the lower deities,
they will cause all that is sought to be fully obtained.
*Svabhā svabhā, eṇuṣe eṇuṣe, kuṭṭape kuṭṭape, svāhā.* This is the divine mantra spoken by Hārītī.
It enables sentient beings to uproot erroneous views and rescue themselves from peril and distress;
they shall be liberated from bandits, kings, and calamities.
Whatever sons or daughters they seek shall all be upright and handsome.
Marriage brings about enemies and creditors;
through this, one attains complete liberation and finds peace in all things.
